scenario: AITA for telling my dad I'm not sticking around? | My parents separated when I was pretty young and my mom was awarded full custody. My father wanted to stay in my life at first, but the courts ruled in favor of my mom controlling visitation until he found a place to live and got a job. He was really bad off back then, and my mom was at least able to make bills. Instead of getting his act together, my father never tried to get involved with me again until recently when my mom died and he accepted custody. He has a house, a job, a GF, and she has a little boy. All living together. I didn't have to move out of state or anything, but it's a good distance from where I've lived my whole life and my best friend was still willing to take the time and gas to come see me. When he got here, my dad was very standoffish and when he left I was told I wasn't allowed to interact at with him at all anymore. I'm sure it's because he's a year older, has face piercings and some tattoos, and does weird styles and colors with his hair. My dad went so far as to lock my social media so I can have no contact. But my best friend is like my *best friend.* We've been through a lot-we grew up poor, we've had our fair share of bullying and family problems. I love my mom, but she wasn't perfect and there was a lot of shit to work through. He is a great guy who's always stood by me, and my dad dismissed him solely on his appearance. I got pissed and told my dad not to expect me to be around in a year when I turn eighteen, and his girlfriend told me I should be ashamed for using that as blackmail. To me, if it's a choice between dad or best friend, I'm going with the guy who has been there with me the whole way. AITA for threatening to bail?

This could lead to further restrictions (e.g., limiting your freedom, moving you, etc.). 2. **The "Year" Threat Might Backfire** - Saying *"I won’t stick around in a year"* could be seen as a ultimatum rather than a boundary. If he takes it personally, he might try to "prove" he’s a better father by being more controlling (e.g., restricting your phone, limiting your friend’s visits, etc.). This could make your life harder in the short term. - A stronger approach might be to **state your needs clearly** (e.g., *"I need to be able to see [friend] without restrictions. If that’s not possible, I’ll need to find a way to live independently sooner."*) rather than making a vague threat. 3. **You Might Lose Out on Future Opportunities** - If you leave abruptly, you could miss out on time with your father *if* he ever changes his mind. But if he’s truly the kind of person who’d rather isolate you than accept your friend, then that’s a cost worth paying. --- ### **What’s *Really* at Stake Here?** This isn’t just about a "bad haircut" or a friend’s tattoos—it’s about **who gets to define what "family" means to you**. Your father’s reaction suggests he’s more interested in: - **Control** (locking your social media, forbidding contact). - **Judgment** (dismissing your friend based on appearance). - **Conditional love** (only showing up when it suited him). Your best friend, on the other hand, has been a **constant, unconditional presence** in your life. That’s a huge difference. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead (If You Want to Stay but Set Boundaries):** If you’re open to it, you could try: 1. **Direct Communication** - Tell your father: *"I love you, but I can’t stay in a place where I’m not allowed to see [friend]. If you can’t respect that, I’ll need to find a way to live independently sooner."* This puts the ball in his court—does he want to keep you, or does he want you to leave? 2. **Document Everything** - If he continues to restrict your freedom (e.g., phone, visits), keep records. Once you turn 18, you’ll have more legal rights to assert independence. 3. **Plan for Independence** - Start looking into housing options, part-time jobs, or other ways to prepare for when you turn 18. The more self-sufficient you are, the less power he has over you. 4. **Lean on Your Friend** - If your friend is truly supportive, they can help you navigate this. Maybe they can visit more often, or even help you find resources (e.g., a job, a place to stay). --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not wrong for valuing your friendship over someone who’s been inconsistent and dismissive. But your threat *might* be more effective if framed as a **demand for respect** rather than a vague ultimatum. Either way, **you’re not obligated to stay in a situation that feels oppressive**, especially when you’re about to turn 18. Would you like help brainstorming ways to communicate this to your father without escalating conflict? Or are you leaning toward leaving sooner rather than later?
